newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Political image, growth hopes boost Russian stocks.
newsitem.headline: Political image, growth hopes boost Russian stocks.

text.p: Russian stocks seem poised for long-term growth amid perceptions that the country is over the worst of its political problems and that economic growth is in sight after years of contraction.

Moscow traders say that the foreign buying has helped to push up the market 50 percent this year, coupled with Russian institutional investors who have moved into stocks after yields on government securities tumbled.
"People still feel comfortable Russia is going to be one of the best performing emerging markets of the year," said Brunswick brokerage director Martin Diggle.
Investors of all nationalities and economic levels are eyeing Russian shares, which promise long-term growth despite the risk of corrections along the way.
The market paused for breath on Wednesday and the Russian Trading System (RTS) index retreated to 306.79 at the close from Tuesday's record close of 312.60.
But traders saw this as only temporary, saying the market was establishing a new level as fresh funds sought shares and many stockholders refused to sell.
Diggle said some foreign investors had taken profits but were holding cash, as they planned to buy again in Russia rather than shifting to a different market.
Investors are chasing both undervalued companies and those expected to grow, analysts say.
Large foreign funds, especially from the United States, believe Russia is politically stable and will see real economic growth, even if not until 1998.

Industrial output rose 0.3 percent year-on-year in January, a month which generally sees economic contraction. This was the first time the January figure had risen since painful economic reforms began in 1992.

Political risk has declined sharply with President Boris Yeltsin's health apparently improving, communist and nationalist anti-reformers quiet, and the conflict in Chechnya fading as Aslan Maskhadov took office as president of the separatist region on Wednesday.
Relatively light buying can also move the Russian market a long way as daily turnover is only about $40 million, albeit up from $25 million at the end of 1996.
Russian institutional investors are now joining Westerners on the stock market as yields on government securities have fallen to about 30 percent from nearly 200 percent early last year.
"Russian investors have nowhere else to go," one trader said.
Christopher Granville, director of research at United City Bank, estimated that Russian institutions controlled up to 30 percent of the free float in some shares.
Average Russians, estimated to hold $20-30 billion in cash, may also be persuaded to buy shares.
"If unit funds develop quickly, they could play a big role and affect the corporate securities market," said Timothy Frost, chairman of the management board of Pioneer First Investment Group.
Pioneer plans to open a domestic equity fund in a month.
On Wednesday there were few sellers, and high demand gave the market little room to fall, said CS First Boston dealer Pavel Naumenko.
"There is demand at these levels which gives reason to believe that the blue chips will fluctuate within a narrow range for the next few days," he said.

Market leader utility UES EESR.RTS bucked the trend on Wednesday, rising to $0.2045, up from Tuesday's closing $0.202, after recovering from earlier losses, and a number of smaller utilities and preferred shares showed gains of 2-3 percent.
